analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale and manufacture of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The bill went no further than the day it was introduced: referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. Weapons and magazines already lawfully owned would be grandfathered: they could stay in circulation and, for weapons, be sold between private parties after a licensed dealer runs a background check. It exempts law enforcement, retired officers, and many specified hunting and sporting firearms, and lets state and local governments fund buy-back programs with existing federal grant money.
analysis.who_benefits: People worried about mass shootings and gun violence in their communities, since the weapons covered are the type most often used in high-casualty public shootings; the Attorney General would also have to publish a public record of crimes committed with covered weapons.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it a crime to knowingly import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon or a large-capacity ammunition feeding device, the categories of firearms and magazines used in many high-casualty mass shootings.

It grandfathers existing weapons and magazines, so current owners keep them, but requires licensed dealers to run a background check before any private sale or transfer of a grandfathered weapon and requires secure storage when a prohibited person could access it.
It directs the Attorney General to keep and publish an annual public record of covered weapons used in crimes, including the outcome of investigations and prosecutions.
It allows state and local governments to use Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funds to pay individuals who surrender a covered weapon under a buy-back program.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and magazine manufacturers lose their largest civilian product lines, licensed dealers lose sales of covered guns, and owners who would have wanted to buy such weapons in the future cannot. Existing owners face new rules: background checks for private weapon sales and a secure-storage requirement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and future buyers

drawbacks.text: The bill grandfathers every assault weapon and magazine already lawfully owned, so millions of covered weapons and magazines remain in circulation; grandfathered weapons can even be resold between private parties after a background check, meaning the banned supply continues to trade for years.

The ban is defined largely by cosmetic features rather than function: a semiautomatic rifle counts if it has any one of a pistol grip, forward grip, folding stock, barrel shroud, threaded barrel, or grenade launcher, which sweeps in firearms many owners use for hunting and recreation; the text also lists hundreds of specific exempted models, creating a line-by-line map that new variants could skirt.

It creates a federal crime of simple possession going forward, so a person who lawfully buys a covered weapon before enactment could commit a crime only by actions after it, but anyone who obtains a covered weapon later faces felony exposure even without a sale or transfer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the weapon types most associated with mass shootings and leaves current owners whole, which keeps the immediate burden low. Its main limits are built in: the grandfather clause means the stock of covered weapons keeps trading for years, and the feature-based definitions invite workarounds and disputes over what counts. The 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban's effects on overall gun crime were debated and modest by most studies, so realistic expectations for crime reduction should be tempered even as the bill addresses high-casualty shootings.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced on January 23, 2023 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day, it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the Assault Weapons Ban of 2023 on January 23, 2023, with 45 original cosponsors listed in the introduction.

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and the action history shows no further activity — no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote — through the end of the Congress.
The bill had 45 cosponsors: 44 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and 1 of its 4 independents; no Republican cosponsored.
The House never considered companion legislation in the record for this bill; the Senate referral was the only action ever taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm and magazine manufacturers and dealers are better off: the market for AR-15-style rifles, other covered semiautomatics, and large-capacity magazines stayed open. Gun owners' existing access is also unchanged, since the ban never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun and magazine makers and sellers

for.name: Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 23, 2023 and sponsored it throughout the Congress.

for.name: 44 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no further action was taken on it after referral to committee.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole independent cosponsor.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote after it was referred to the Judiciary Committee; no committee action appears in the bill's history.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal assault weapons bans of this kind, lobbying against their consideration and passage.

against.name: Firearms and ammunition industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against restrictions on the sale of semiautomatic rifles and high-capacity magazines, the industry's core civilian products.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 cosponsors were Democrats or an independent; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote in either chamber.

industries.industry: Firearm manufacturers (AR-15 and AK-pattern rifles, covered pistols and shotguns)
industries.note: The bill names specific products from major makers — including Daniel Defense, Smith & Wesson, Sturm Ruger, Sig Sauer, Bushmaster, and Kel-Tec — and bans their import, sale, and manufacture, eliminating the industry's fastest-growing civilian product line. The industry's interest in keeping these weapons on sale runs against the bill's public-safety purpose.

Manufacture and sale of any magazine holding more than 10 rounds would become a federal crime, shutting down the standard-capacity magazine business for civilian sales. Existing magazines are grandfathered, so the ban bites only on future supply.

Dealers lose all sales of covered weapons and new large-capacity magazines, but grandfathered weapons remain legal to sell, and every private-party transfer of a grandfathered weapon must now run through a licensed dealer's background check — a small new revenue stream with compliance duties.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and security services
industries.note: The bill fully exempts federal, state, and campus law enforcement, retired officers, and nuclear-materials security from the ban, so the agencies' access to these firearms is untouched while civilian access is cut off.
